full_text_en:
Shandong Hanlin Biotechnology Co., Ltd. v. China National Intellectual Property Administration, et al.

Administrative Dispute over Invalidation of Invention Patent Right

[Ruling Summary]

I. The patent system protects technical solutions that utilize the laws of nature to solve technical problems, not the laws of nature themselves. Therefore, when examining whether a claim clearly defines the scope of patent protection, the content to be reviewed is whether the claim clearly defines the technical solution itself under patent protection, rather than whether the laws of nature utilized by the technical solution have been clearly elaborated and defined.

II. Where a person illegally applies for a patent using another person's technological achievements, and after the patent right from such illegal application is lawfully returned to the other person, that person then files a request for invalidation of the said patent right, such conduct obviously violates the principle of good faith and shall not be supported by the people's court.

Supreme People's Court
Administrative Judgment

(2020) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Xing Zhong No. 564

Appellant (defendant at first instance): China National Intellectual Property Administration. Address: No. 6, Xitucheng Road, Jimenqiao, Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Shen Changyu, Director General of the Administration.

Agent ad litem: Hou Yao, Examiner of the Administration.

Agent ad litem: Zhao Xin, Examiner of the Administration.

Appellant (third party at first instance): Shanghai Cathay Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Address: 4th Floor, Building 5, No. 1690, Cailun Road, China (Shanghai) Pilot Free Trade Zone.

Legal Representative: Liu Xiucai, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Qiulin, Lawyer of Beijing Yuntian Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Li Debao, Lawyer of Beijing Yuntian Law Firm.

Respondent (plaintiff at first instance): Shandong Hanlin Biotechnology Co., Ltd. Address: No. 1, Emei Road, (Development Zone), Laiyang City, Shandong Province.

Legal Representative: Cao Wubo, Executive Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Zhao Rui, Lawyer of Beijing Gaowen Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wang Mingxi, Lawyer of Beijing Gaowen Law Firm.

In the administrative dispute over invalidation of invention patent right between appellants China National Intellectual Property Administration and Shanghai Cathay Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Cathay Company) and respondent Shandong Hanlin Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hanlin Company), the appellants appealed to this Court against the administrative judgment (2019) Jing 73 Xing Chu No. 7946 rendered by the Beijing Intellectual Property Court on July 15, 2020. After filing the appeal on November 5, 2020, this Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and held a public hearing on May 28, 2021. Agents ad litem of appellant China National Intellectual Property Administration Hou Yao and Zhao Xin, agents ad litem of appellant Cathay Company Zhang Qiulin and Li Debao, and agents ad litem of respondent Hanlin Company Zhao Rui and Wang Mingxi appeared in court for the hearing. The case has now been concluded.

Grounds for the appeal of China National Intellectual Property Administration: 1. To set aside the original judgment; 2. To uphold the No. 39674 Review Decision on Invalidity Declaration Request (hereinafter referred to as the decision under appeal) made by China National Intellectual Property Administration. Facts and reasons: The invention patent titled "Refining Process for Producing Long-Chain Dicarboxylic Acid by Biological Fermentation" with patent number 201010160266.4 (hereinafter referred to as the patent in suit) complies with Articles 26(3), 26(4), and 22(3) of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (as amended in 2008) (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Law), and the original judgment erred in finding otherwise. (I) For terms in the claims, they should be understood from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account common general knowledge in the technical field. The term "very low solubility of long-chain dicarboxylic acid" in the claims of the patent in suit is common general knowledge in the art, and all parties have no objection to this. On this basis, a person of ordinary skill in the art could not mechanically interpret "high-temperature water crystallization" as a strict "crystallization" in the conventional sense. The original judgment, starting purely from the literal meaning, considered that it should first be interpreted as "using high-temperature water as a solvent to completely dissolve the crystals obtained in step (2) and then precipitate them in crystalline form, or without using a solvent, completely melt and then recrystallize," which deviates from the basic understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art. (II) The description of step (3) in the specification and claim 1 of the patent in suit is clear. By reading the contents of the specification and combining common general knowledge in the art, a person of ordinary skill in the art can understand that the accurate meaning of the "crystallization and separation" step performed in the "high-temperature water crystallization tank" is "in the tank equipment, under the action of high-temperature water, obtaining and separating dicarboxylic acid products in crystalline form." This step is not strictly a "solvent crystallization" or "melt crystallization" method, and its meaning differs from that of "crystallization" in step (2). (III) Cathay Company's interpretation of the technical solution does not present any inconsistency. In the invalidity declaration request involved in this case, when interpreting the material state in step (3), Cathay Company argued that under the combined action of high temperature and water, the dicarboxylic acid in this step is in a dispersed state of "partial dissolution-melt-suspension." This interpretation is basically consistent with the understanding of a person of ordinary skill in the art. In the invalidity declaration request corresponding to the No. 42594 Review Decision on Invalidity Declaration Request (after the decision under appeal was made, Hanlin Company filed another invalidity declaration request against the patent in suit on June 21, 2019, and China National Intellectual Property Administration made the No. 42594 Review Decision on Invalidity Declaration Request on December 29, 2019, upholding the validity of the patent in suit; hereinafter referred to as the No. 42594 Decision), Cathay Company made a statement that "there is no melting in step (3) of claim 1 of the patent in suit," the purpose of which was only to negate that step (3) of the patent in suit is a specific crystallization method such as "melt crystallization," and this does not contradict its statement in this case. The original judgment actually expanded the patentee's assertion to negate that "there may be partially melted dicarboxylic acid in step (3)" and thus found it contradictory to the patentee's previous statement that the patent in suit involves a "dispersed state of partial dissolution-melt-suspension." This finding is inconsistent with the facts. (IV) Relevant facts have been confirmed in judgments of courts at various levels. Since 2012, Cathay Company and Hanlin Company have been litigating around the patent in suit and related patent rights in courts at various levels across the country. In the final judgments of the above disputes, a copy of a SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) drafted on October 3, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as the 2003 SOP) was involved, which recorded a production process substantially identical to claim 1 of the patent in suit. This evidence was used by the courts as the basis for determining that the actual inventor of the patent in suit should be an employee of Cathay Company. According to the 2003 SOP, the operation in step (3) of claim 1 of the patent in suit has been referred to as the "high-temperature water crystallization" step since the beginning of the invention. Both the current patentee Cathay Company and the former patentee Hanlin Company should have been clear about the technical meaning of this term and the specific operational details therein; in actual production, this is how the operation was performed. This further confirms that the scope of protection of the claims of the patent in suit is clear, and there is no situation where the claim terms are unclear, leading to the inability to implement the technical solution. The patent in suit complies with Articles 26(3) and 26(4) of the Patent Law.

Grounds for the appeal of Cathay Company: To set aside the original judgment, uphold the decision under appeal, and order Hanlin Company to bear the litigation costs of both instances. Facts and reasons: (I) The technical solution defined by claim 1 of the patent in suit is clear. 1. Claim 1 has clearly and completely described the refining process for producing long-chain dicarboxylic acid by biological fermentation, including 4 steps, with specific operational methods and conditions for each step. 2. Step (3) of claim 1 clearly records the source of the material, the equipment into which it is placed, the controlled temperature range and time, and the temperature range for cooling. A person of ordinary skill in the art, based on the above description, can perform the specific operation and understand its boundaries. 3. Based on the common general knowledge that long-chain dicarboxylic acid has low solubility in water, a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand that "high-temperature water crystallization" in step (3) should not be a process of "completely dissolving the dicarboxylic acid in water and then completely crystallizing it again by cooling." 4. The "complete crystallization" mentioned in step (3) means that after cooling, the dicarboxylic acid dissolved in water substantially precipitates out in crystalline form due to decreased solubility, not "complete dissolution followed by complete crystallization," and the claim does not impose any limitation on the solubility of long-chain dicarboxylic acid. (II) The scope of protection of claim 1 can also be clearly defined through the specification of the patent in suit. The specification of the patent in suit describes in detail the background art, the objective of the invention, the technical solution, and the technical effects achieved. The technical solution described in the summary of the invention is consistent with claim 1. In the detailed description, specific examples are given, and step (3) provides specific point values for controlled temperature, holding time, and cooling temperature. The specific operation process described also falls within the scope of claim 1. Additionally, technical effect data on total acid content, single acid content, total nitrogen content, Fe ion content, ash content, and moisture content are provided, and comparisons with existing technologies are made. Therefore, the specification provides a clear and complete description of the invention. A person of ordinary skill in the art, after reading the specification, knows how to implement it and can clearly define the scope of protection of claim 1. (III) The reason the Patent Law requires the scope of protection of a claim to be "clear" is to define the boundary of the patent right, enabling a person of ordinary skill in the art to clearly know which technical solutions will fall within the scope of protection of the patent right and thus constitute infringement, and which technical solutions will not fall within the scope of protection and can be avoided and freely practiced. The original judgment, in stating that "given the low solubility of long-chain dicarboxylic acid in water, the crystallization process described in step (3) is clearly illogical from a technical perspective and has no practical significance in production," misunderstood the meaning of Article 26(4) of the Patent Law, failing to accurately grasp the basic meaning of that provision. In summary, the scope of protection of claim 1 of the patent in suit is clear, the specification is sufficiently disclosed, and the patent in suit complies with Articles 26(4) and 26(3) of the Patent Law. (IV) Since the scope of protection of claim 1 is clear and there are multiple distinguishing technical features between claim 1 and the evidence submitted by Hanlin Company, a person of ordinary skill in the art could not obviously obtain the technical solution of claim 1, and therefore claim 1 possesses inventive step.

Hanlin Company argued: (I) The two terms "water" and "crystallization" in step (3) of claim 1 of the patent in suit are obviously contradictory and cannot be reasonably explained, resulting in an unclear scope of protection, in violation of Article 26(4) of the Patent Law. 1. "Crystallization" has a common meaning in the chemical field: a hot saturated solution, upon cooling, causes the solute to become supersaturated due to decreased solubility, thereby precipitating in crystalline form. The specification of the patent in suit does not provide a special definition for "crystallization," so the common meaning should be used to interpret "crystallization" in step (3). 2. The terms "primary crystallization," "complete crystallization of the material," and "crystallized material" in step (2) of claim 1 all use the common meaning of "crystallization." According to the interpretive rule that "the same term in the same claim should have the same meaning," the term "crystallization" in step (3) should also be interpreted according to its ordinary meaning in the chemical field. Therefore, step (3) protects a technical solution of "using water as a solvent to achieve purification through crystallization of the dicarboxylic acid." 3. From the literal meaning of the claim, step (3) is a method for purifying dicarboxylic acid particles by performing a crystallization process in water. The description of step (3) in Examples 1, 2, and 3 of the specification is substantially consistent with the wording of claim 1. 4. Because dodecanedioic acid is very slightly soluble in water, the technical solution of "using water as a solvent to achieve purification through crystallization of the dicarboxylic acid" requires a large amount of high-temperature water and large crystallization tanks and other supporting equipment, and is only theoretically feasible. In practice, not only would industrial production not adopt it, but even laboratories would not use it. (II) Cathay Company's provision of three different interpretations of step (3) in two invalidity declaration procedures also demonstrates that the scope of protection of the patent in suit is unclear. 1. In this case, Cathay Company argued that the dicarboxylic acid in step (3) is in a dispersed state of "partial dissolution-melt-suspension." "Partial dissolution" is due to residual acetic acid from step (2) dissolving some dicarboxylic acid particles, and "melt" is because the dicarboxylic acid particles contain impurities that lower the melting point. 2. In the invalidity declaration request corresponding to the No. 42594 Decision, Cathay Company argued that step (3) "high-temperature water crystallization" is, like step (2), a crystallization process. This interpretation is consistent with the literal interpretation of claim 1 of the patent in suit. 3. In the invalidity declaration request corresponding to the No. 42594 Decision, Cathay Company further argued that step (3) is a "washing process accompanied by a crystallization phenomenon," and retracted its previous views regarding partial dissolution due to residual acetic acid, existence of melting, and being a crystallization process. (III) In the two invalidity declaration procedures, China National Intellectual Property Administration endorsed Cathay Company's first and third interpretations respectively, which also indicates that the scope of protection of the patent in suit is unclear. 1. In the decision under appeal, China National Intellectual Property Administration endorsed Cathay Company's argument that "the dicarboxylic acid in this step is actually in a dispersed state of 'partial dissolution-melt-suspension.'" However, in the No. 42594 Decision, China National Intellectual Property Administration considered that "there is no melting situation" in step (3) of claim 1 of the patent in suit. 2. In the No. 42594 Decision, China National Intellectual Property Administration characterized step (3) as a "washing process accompanied by a crystallization phenomenon." However, due to the very low solubility of long-chain dicarboxylic acid in water, achieving crystallization of trace amounts of dicarboxylic acid dissolved in water would require significant time and energy. Therefore, this technical solution of first forming a supersaturated solution and then achieving "recrystallization" of long-chain dicarboxylic acid is not feasible and is a technical solution that a person of ordinary skill in the art would clearly exclude. (IV) In the appeal briefs in this case, China National Intellectual Property Administration and Cathay Company gave opposite interpretations of "crystallization" in step (3), which also demonstrates that the scope of protection of step (3) is unclear. China National Intellectual Property Administration argued in its appeal brief that the same term "crystallization" in steps (2) and (3) of claim 1 has different meanings, while Cathay Company argued in its appeal brief that "crystallization" in steps (2) and (3) is consistent. This alone is sufficient to determine that the scope of protection of step (3) is unclear. (V) If Cathay Company implemented "high-temperature water crystallization" in step (3) and achieved the "dispersed state of partial dissolution-melt-suspension," that would be a major technological breakthrough in the field. However, the specification does not describe how to achieve the "dispersed state of partial dissolution-melt-suspension," which constitutes insufficient disclosure of the specification.

Hanlin Company filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, which accepted the case on July 8, 2019. Hanlin Company's claims: To set aside the decision under appeal and order China National Intellectual Property Administration to render a new decision. Facts and reasons: The patent in suit does not comply with Articles 26(3), 26(4), and 22(3) of the Patent Law. Claim 1 and the specification of the patent in suit do not record the amount of water used in step (3) and the relationship with the crystallized material obtained in step (2). A person of ordinary skill in the art cannot achieve the technical purpose of improving purity based on the description in the specification, so claim 1 does not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law. Based on substantially the same reasons as above, the specification of the patent in suit does not comply with Article 26(3) of the Patent Law. As for the inventive step of claim 1, regarding distinguishing feature (i), based on Annex 2's disclosure of dissolving crude dicarboxylic acid with acetic acid and using activated carbon for decolorization, a person of ordinary skill in the art would be motivated in practice to adjust the amount of acetic acid and the water content of the crude dicarboxylic acid, and using a plate-and-frame filter press is also a conventional choice in the field. Regarding distinguishing feature (ii), based on the technical solution of Annex 2, a person of ordinary skill in the art would easily conceive of using the two-crystallization scheme disclosed in Annex 3. Specific steps and conditions can be determined according to actual needs without inventive effort. Regarding distinguishing feature (iii), high-temperature water crystallization is essentially a reverse extraction, a common purification technique used by a person of ordinary skill in the art. Regarding distinguishing feature (iv), choosing to dry in a flash dryer is a conventional choice in the field and does not produce unexpected technical effects.

China National Intellectual Property Administration argued at first instance: It adhered to the opinions expressed in the decision under appeal. The decision under appeal had clear factual findings, correct application of law, and lawful review procedures. Hanlin Company's grounds for litigation could not stand. It requested the court to dismiss Hanlin Company's claims.

Cathay Company stated at first instance: It agreed with the opinions expressed in the decision under appeal and requested the court to dismiss Hanlin Company's claims.

The court of first instance found the following facts:

The filing date of the patent in suit was April 30, 2010, and the patentee was Cathay Company. The claims as published upon grant of the patent in suit were as follows: "1. A refining process for producing long-chain dicarboxylic acid by biological fermentation, characterized in that the refining steps include: (1) decolorization and filtration; (2) primary crystallization and separation; (3) high-temperature water crystallization and separation; (4) drying; the said step (1) decolorization and filtration: placing crude dicarboxylic acid into a decolorization tank, with a water content of 5 to 12 wt%, adding 0.05 to 0.2 wt% of activated carbon, with a mass ratio of solvent (converted to 100% content) to dicarboxylic acid of 3.0 to 2.0:1, decolorizing at a temperature of 85 to 100 degrees Celsius for 20 to 90 minutes, then filtering through a plate-and-frame filter press to obtain a clear dicarboxylic acid solution; the said step (2) primary crystallization and separation: placing the clear dicarboxylic acid solution obtained in step (1) into a primary crystallization tank, cooling to 75 to 85 degrees Celsius, holding the temperature for 1 to 2 hours, then cooling to 25 to 35 degrees Celsius, after the material is completely crystallized, separating the crystallized material using a centrifuge; the said step (3) high-temperature water crystallization and separation: placing the crystallized material obtained in step (2) into a high-temperature water crystallization tank, controlling the temperature at 70 to 100 degrees Celsius, holding the temperature for 120 minutes, then cooling to 30 to 50 degrees Celsius, after the material is completely crystallized, separating the crystallized material using a centrifuge to obtain wet dicarboxylic acid; the said step (4) drying: drying the wet dicarboxylic acid obtained in step (3) in a flash dryer to obtain a refined long-chain dicarboxylic acid product; the solvent in the said step (1) is an acetic acid solution with a content of 90% or more."

On November 14, 2018, Hanlin Company filed a request for invalidation of the patent with the Patent Reexamination Board of the former State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board), on the grounds that the description of the patent did not comply with Article 26(3) of the Patent Law and that claim 1 was unclear, thus not complying with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law, requesting a declaration of invalidity of claim 1 of the patent. At the same time, it submitted the following Annex 1:

Annex 1: "Research Progress in the Preparation and Refinement of Long-Chain Dicarboxylic Acids," by Liu Ya et al., *Modern Chemical Industry*, Volume 38, Issue 8, pp. 43-47, August 31, 2018.

On December 3, 2018, the Patent Reexamination Board accepted the request for invalidation and established a collegial panel for review.

On December 14, 2018, Hanlin Company submitted a statement of opinion and the following Annex 2 and Annex 3, arguing that claim 1 of the patent did not comply with Article 22(3) of the Patent Law in view of the combination of Annex 2 and Annex 3:

Annex 2: CN101121653A, publication date February 13, 2008.

Annex 3: CN1570124A, publication date January 26, 2005.

On March 18, 2019, the Patent Reexamination Board held an oral hearing. During the oral hearing, Hanlin Company submitted Annex 4 (*Encyclopedia of Chemical Engineering*, Volume 3, Chemical Industry Press, first edition in 1993, cover, publication information page, table of contents page v, pp. 1039, 1054-1060) as evidence of common general knowledge, to prove the same facts as Annex 1, i.e., that long-chain dicarboxylic acids are insoluble in water. Kaisai Company acknowledged the authenticity of Annexes 1-4 but argued that the publication date of Annex 1 was later than the filing date of the patent and thus could not be used as prior art or evidence of common general knowledge.

On March 29, 2019, the Patent Reexamination Board issued the contested decision. The contested decision recorded:

1. Regarding whether the patent was sufficiently disclosed and whether the claims were clear.

Hanlin Company argued that: (1) The key equipment used in step (3) of claim 1 of the patent, the "high-temperature water crystallization tank," was itself ambiguous. Without specific conditions such as the proportions of solvent, pH value, water, and crystallized material, it was unclear how this step was carried out. Even if the solvent was considered to be high-temperature water, it was common knowledge in the art that long-chain dicarboxylic acids are insoluble in water. (2) In step (1), the base for the percentage of water content, the base for the percentage of activated carbon content, and the mass ratio of solvent to dicarboxylic acid were not specified. (3) The effects claimed in the patent, namely "good light transmittance" and "high thermal stability," were not foreseeable by a person of ordinary skill in the art based on the technical solution of the patent. Therefore, the description of the patent was insufficiently disclosed, not complying with Article 26(3) of the Patent Law. Based on the same reasons as in (3) above, the technical solution of claim 1 and its scope of protection were unclear, not complying with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law.

The Patent Reexamination Board held that, according to the description of the patent, the current technology employed by manufacturers of long-chain dicarboxylic acids could only produce crude dicarboxylic acid (referred to as P-grade product). However, the crude dicarboxylic acid had low monocarboxylic acid content, poor thermal stability, low purity, high ash and iron salt content, and its product quality did not meet polymer-grade quality standards, failing to satisfy customers' high-quality demands, which greatly limited the application range of long-chain dicarboxylic acids. The object of the present invention was to overcome the deficiencies of the prior art and provide a refining process for producing long-chain dicarboxylic acids by biological fermentation. The long-chain dicarboxylic acids produced by this refining process had characteristics such as high acid production level, low production cost, good product quality, and complete variety, greatly expanding the development space for downstream products of long-chain dicarboxylic acids. ... The beneficial effects of the present invention were: the refining process for producing long-chain dicarboxylic acids by biological fermentation included the steps of: (1) decolorization and filtration; (2) primary crystallization and separation; (3) high-temperature water crystallization and separation; (4) drying. The resulting long-chain dicarboxylic acid products had high monocarboxylic acid content, good light transmittance, and high thermal stability, meeting the needs of different customers and could be used in the production of high-grade spices, high-performance engineering plastics, high-temperature dielectrics, high-grade hot melt adhesives, cold-resistant plasticizers, high-grade lubricants, high-grade paints and coatings, etc., greatly expanding the development space for downstream products of long-chain dicarboxylic acids. In the specific embodiments, the patent used different refining process conditions, performing refining processes in Examples 1-3 to obtain refined long-chain dicarboxylic acids, and measured the product quality indicators of dodecanedioic acid and tridecanedioic acid produced in Examples 1, 2, and 3, comparing them with crude dicarboxylic acid. Thus, the object of the invention was to provide a refining method for treating crude dicarboxylic acid to obtain a product with higher purity, the method comprising four steps: (1) decolorization and filtration; (2) primary crystallization and separation; (3) high-temperature water crystallization and separation; (4) drying. In paragraphs [0008] to [0012] of the description, the patent provided detailed specific operating conditions for the above four steps. In Examples 1-3, by further selecting operating conditions, a white powdery dicarboxylic acid product was obtained, and the product's total acid content, monocarboxylic acid content, total nitrogen content, Fe ion content, ash content, and moisture content were measured. Compared with products obtained by the prior art, various indicators were improved.

The Patent Reexamination Board specifically responded to the reasons asserted by Hanlin Company, holding that: First, step (3) of the refining process of the patent was high-temperature water crystallization and separation. In this step, the material obtained from step (2) after primary crystallization was treated in a high-temperature water crystallization tank, controlling temperature and holding time, then cooling for crystallization, and separating the wet dicarboxylic acid product using a centrifuge. It was common knowledge to a person of ordinary skill in the art that the solubility of dicarboxylic acids in water was low. For example, the solubility of a 10-carbon dicarboxylic acid (sebacic acid) in water was 0.1 g/100 g, and the solubility of dodecanedioic acid at 23 degrees Celsius was 0.003 g/100 g, rising to 0.37 g/100 g at 100 degrees Celsius. ... Therefore, although chemical products generally exhibited increased solubility with rising temperature, a person of ordinary skill in the art could also infer that the "high-temperature water crystallization" in step (3) should not be a conventional recrystallization process in which water was used as a solvent, the dicarboxylic acid was completely dissolved in water, and crystals were reprecipitated by cooling. Furthermore, because the material used in this step was impure dicarboxylic acid, including residual solvent, moisture, and impurities not removed from the previous step, after the dicarboxylic acid in this step was held at 70-100 degrees Celsius for 120 minutes, the crystallization tank should contain a relatively complex solid-liquid mixed system, which would not be exactly the same as the state of pure dicarboxylic acid dissolved in water. Kaisai Company also argued during the oral hearing that in this step, the dicarboxylic acid was actually in a dispersed state of "partial dissolution-melting-suspension." Therefore, Hanlin Company's reason for questioning the feasibility of this step on the grounds of the low solubility of dicarboxylic acid was untenable. Moreover, choosing the container for performing the above process as a high-temperature water crystallization tank according to the appropriate production scale and process requirements, as well as selecting the amount of water used, was within the capability of a person of ordinary skill in the art. Additionally, there was no evidence indicating that this step required the presence of other solvents or pH adjustment.

Second, step (1) specified the water content of the raw material crude dicarboxylic acid. A person of ordinary skill in the art would generally understand that the water content should be based on the crude dicarboxylic acid. Regarding the amount of activated carbon added, a person of ordinary skill in the art would generally understand that it should be based on the entire system. Regarding the amount of solvent added, claim 1 and the description of the patent clearly stated that it was added according to the mass ratio to the dicarboxylic acid. The term "dicarboxylic acid" here was textually distinguished from the "crude dicarboxylic acid" in that step. Measuring the dicarboxylic acid content in the crude dicarboxylic acid was achievable for a person of ordinary skill in the art. Kaisai Company's statements in its written submissions and during the oral hearing were also consistent with the conventional understanding in the art.

Third, as previously stated, the description of the patent already provided the indicators of the product treated by the process of the patent, as well as comparative results with products of the prior art. Therefore, it was also foreseeable that the product had the technical effects of "good light transmittance" and "high thermal stability" compared with prior art products.

Thus, for the technical solution of claim 1, the description of the patent provided the raw materials, process steps, and process conditions used in the method. There was no evidence that a person of ordinary skill in the art could not implement the solution according to the above description, or could not solve the technical problem to be solved by the patent. Hanlin Company's reasons that the description of the patent did not comply with Article 26(3) of the Patent Law were all untenable. Similarly, the reason that claim 1 did not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law due to an unclear scope of protection was also untenable.

2. Regarding inventiveness.

Annex 2 related to a method for producing long-chain dicarboxylic acids by fermentation using fatty acid esters or fatty acid salts as raw materials, which involved the extraction and purification of dicarboxylic acids: adding alkali to the fermentation broth to adjust the pH to 7-11, heating to 60-100 degrees Celsius, then separating the bacterial cells, dicarboxylic acid clear liquid, and residual fermentation substrate using centrifugation or membrane filtration. Depending on the situation, activated carbon not exceeding 5% of the volume of the clear liquid was added to the obtained dicarboxylic acid clear liquid, decolorized at 50-95 degrees Celsius for 10-180 minutes, filtered to remove activated carbon, then the decolorized liquid was heated to 50-100 degrees Celsius, and acid was used to adjust the pH to 2-5 for acidification crystallization. The acidified crystallization liquid was then filter-pressed to obtain crude long-chain dicarboxylic acid. The crude long-chain dicarboxylic acid was dissolved using an organic solvent solution. After the dicarboxylic acid was fully dissolved, activated carbon not exceeding 5% of the total volume of the solution was added, and the mixture was heated to 60-100 degrees Celsius for decolorization for 10-180 minutes. After decolorization, the mixture was filtered while hot, the clear liquid was cooled to 10-40 degrees Celsius to crystallize the long-chain dicarboxylic acid, and the product was collected by centrifugation or plate and frame filtration, washed multiple times with distilled water, and dried to obtain the finished product (see claim 11 of Annex 2 and the second-to-last paragraph on page 3 of the description). ... The solvents used could be alcohols (methanol, ethanol, isopropanol, n-butanol), acids (acetic acid), ketones (acetone), esters (ethyl acetate, butyl acetate), etc.

Annex 3 related to a method for producing normal long-chain dicarboxylic acids by fermentation, the method comprising: 1) fermentation conversion: using C9-C18 alkanes or fatty acids as substrates, converting them into corresponding long-chain dicarboxylic acids by microbial fermentation; 2) pretreatment of the fermentation broth: adding alkali to the fermentation broth to adjust the pH to 8-10, heating to 60-100 degrees Celsius, then separating bacterial cells, dicarboxylic acid clear liquid, and residual fermentation substrate using centrifugation or membrane filtration; depending on the situation, 0-5% activated carbon was added to the obtained dicarboxylic acid clear liquid, decolorized at 60-95 degrees Celsius for 20-180 minutes, filtered to remove activated carbon, then the decolorized liquid was heated to 60-100 degrees Celsius, and H2SO4 was used to adjust the pH to 2-5 for acidification crystallization. The acidified crystallization liquid was then filter-pressed to obtain crude dicarboxylic acid; 3) purification by secondary solvent crystallization: the obtained crude dicarboxylic acid was put into a certain proportion of solvent, which could be alcohols (methanol, ethanol, isopropanol, n-butanol), acids (acetic acid), ketones (acetone), esters (ethyl acetate, butyl acetate), etc., heated to dissolve, held at 60-100 degrees Celsius for 30-180 minutes, then cooled for crystallization, solid-liquid separation, and dried to obtain the product.

The target processed in claim 1 of the patent was crude dicarboxylic acid solid with a water content of 5-12 wt%, which corresponded to the "crude long-chain dicarboxylic acid obtained by filtering the acidified crystallization liquid" in Annex 2 and Annex 3. During the oral hearing, Kaisai Company also acknowledged this. Therefore, the correspondence between the processing steps of claim 1 of the patent and the steps of Annex 2 and Annex 3 was as follows:

The differences between the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent and that disclosed by Annex 2 were: (1) Annex 2 did not disclose the water content of the crude dicarboxylic acid, the amount of acetic acid solvent, and the filtration device in step (1) of the patent; (2) Annex 2 did not disclose the two-step cooling to obtain crystals and the specific conditions in step (2) of the patent; (3) Annex 2 did not disclose step (3) of the patent; (4) Annex 2 did not disclose the flash dryer in step (4) of the patent.

Based on the above description of the patent, the object of the patent was to obtain a dicarboxylic acid product with higher purity. In Purification Example 11 on page 11 of the description of Annex 2, using acetic acid as a solvent, a dicarboxylic acid product with a purity of 98.9% was obtained. Therefore, the technical problem actually solved by the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent was improving the purity of the dicarboxylic acid product.

As shown in the table above, Annex 3 also did not disclose the above differences (1) to (4). Regarding the purification of dicarboxylic acid, it disclosed even less information than Annex 2. As previously stated, due to the low water solubility of dicarboxylic acids, a person of ordinary skill in the art also had no motivation to introduce the high-temperature water crystallization step of step (3) of the patent into the dicarboxylic acid purification process to improve the yield of dicarboxylic acid. Therefore, a person of ordinary skill in the art could not obviously obtain the technical solution of claim 1 of the patent based on the above prior art. Hanlin Company's reason that claim 1 lacked inventiveness in view of the combination of Annex 2 and Annex 3 was untenable.

Hanlin Company argued that in Annex 2, "decolorizing the dicarboxylic acid clear liquid with activated carbon," "acidification crystallization," "dissolving in organic solvent and decolorizing with activated carbon," and "drying" corresponded sequentially to steps (1) to (4) of claim 1 of the patent. Therefore, the differences between the two were some specific conditions in the method of the patent, such as amounts, times, temperatures, etc. These features were either easily conceivable by a person of ordinary skill in the art, or were disclosed in Example 30 of Annex 3, while the high-temperature water crystallization step (3) should be understood as a step that could not be implemented in the art.

In response, the Patent Reexamination Board held that, first, as previously stated, the first activated carbon decolorization step in Annex 2 was performed on the dicarboxylic acid clear liquid, the target of which was the dicarboxylic acid clear liquid after filtering out the bacterial cells from the fermentation broth. According to the fermentation method and fermentation preparation examples in the description of Annex 2 (pages 5-7), the culture medium in the fermentation tank was mainly made with water. This was completely different from the system obtained by dissolving the crude dicarboxylic acid in over 90% acetic acid in step (1) of the patent. Therefore, the correspondence between the steps of Annex 2 and the steps of the patent should be as shown in the table above.

Further examining Example 30 of Annex 3, it related to solvent refining of crude dicarboxylic acid, including: crude dicarboxylic acid DC12 250 g, add acetic acid 1000 ml, heat to 90 degrees Celsius to dissolve the dicarboxylic acid, hold for 90 minutes, cool to 15 degrees Celsius within 1 hour for crystallization, filter, add 800 ml of acetic acid to the primary crystallized product, heat to 80 degrees Celsius to dissolve the dicarboxylic acid, hold for 60 minutes, cool to 15 degrees Celsius within 2 hours for crystallization, filter, dry, product 204 g. ... Thus, Example 30 actually belonged to step 3' in the method of Annex 3, i.e., "secondary solvent crystallization refining," except that Example 30 repeated the solvent crystallization twice. Therefore, this example and step 3' should correspond to step (1) of the patent. That is to say, although Example 30 of Annex 3 disclosed some information related to the above difference (1), such as the amount of solvent, it still did not provide any suggestion regarding the other differences, especially difference (3).

The patent achieved the object of improving the purity of the dicarboxylic acid product by introducing a high-temperature water crystallization step into the dicarboxylic acid purification process and combining it with the process parameters of other steps. Therefore, the Patent Reexamination Board did not support Hanlin Company's arguments.

During the original trial hearing of this case, Hanlin Company stated that it had no objection to the contested decision's description of the content disclosed in Annex 2 and Annex 3, but did not accept the contested decision's determination of the correspondence between the processing steps of claim 1 and the steps of Annex 2 and Annex 3. In this case, Hanlin Company argued that the description of the patent did not comply with Article 26(3) of the Patent Law, claim 1 did not comply with Article 26(4) of the Patent Law, and claim 1 lacked inventiveness in view of the combination of Annex 2 and Annex 3.

The court of first instance held:

First, the high-temperature water crystallization should be understood from the limitation of claim 1. Generally, identical technical terms in the claims of a patent have the same technical meaning, while different technical terms have different technical meanings. It is common knowledge to a person of ordinary skill in the art that "crystallization" refers to the process of reducing the solubility of a solute by evaporating the solvent or lowering the temperature based on the difference in solubility of each component in the mixture in a solvent, thereby causing crystals to precipitate. Step (2) of claim 1 was "primary crystallization, separation," specifically "place the dicarboxylic acid clear liquid obtained in step (1) into a primary crystallization tank, cool to 75-85 degrees Celsius, hold for 1-2 hours, then cool to 25-35 degrees Celsius. After the material is completely crystallized, separate the crystallized material using a centrifuge." In combination with step (1) and the description of the patent, a person of ordinary skill in the art could understand that step (2) of claim 1 was a common crystallization operation in the art. Correspondingly, step (3) of claim 1 was "high-temperature water crystallization, separation," specifically "place the crystallized material obtained in step (2) into a high-temperature water crystallization tank, control the temperature at 70-100 degrees Celsius, hold for 120 minutes, then cool to 30-50 degrees Celsius. After the material is completely crystallized, separate the crystallized material using a centrifuge to obtain wet dicarboxylic acid product." At the same time, Examples 1-3 of the description of the patent only specified the temperatures as "70 degrees Celsius, 30 degrees Celsius," "85 degrees Celsius, 40 degrees Celsius," and "100 degrees Celsius, 50 degrees Celsius," respectively, with the rest being consistent with the text of claim 1. Obviously, neither the specific limitation of step (3) of claim 1 nor the content disclosed in Examples 1-3 of the description recorded the addition of any solvent other than water or the need to adjust pH in step (3). Under these circumstances, a person of ordinary skill in the art would generally understand that no "solvent" other than water was added in this step, nor was there any operation for pH adjustment. Therefore, since the description of the patent did not explain the term "crystallization" in step (3) in a manner different from its ordinary meaning in the art, the same term "crystallization" and "complete crystallization" in steps (2) and (3) of claim 1 should have the same meaning. That is to say, step (3) of claim 1, similar to step (2), should also be a conventional crystallization operation process, i.e., step (3) used water as a solvent to achieve the purpose of purification through the crystallization of dicarboxylic acids.

Second, the high-temperature water crystallization should be understood in the context of the overall technical solution. A claim is an expression of a technical solution, and technically illogical or meaningless technical solutions are generally not within the scope of protection of a claim. In this case, the specification of the patent states: "The purpose of the present invention is to overcome the deficiencies of the prior art and provide a refining process for producing long-chain dicarboxylic acids by biological fermentation. The long-chain dicarboxylic acids produced by this refining process have the characteristics of high acid production level, low production cost, good product quality, and complete variety, greatly expanding the development space for downstream products of long-chain dicarboxylic acids." It can be seen that the long-chain dicarboxylic acid refining process described in the patent is specifically applied to industrial production and has the advantage of low production cost. However, it is publicly known in the art (see Exhibit 4) that long-chain dicarboxylic acids have low solubility in water. For example, the solubility of dodecanedioic acid in water is 0.003 g/100 g at 23°C and 0.37 g/100 g at 100°C. If step (3) of claim 1 were understood as a conventional crystallization operation, it would require a large amount of high-temperature water and huge crystallization tanks and other supporting equipment, which is clearly not suitable for industrial production and contradicts the stated purpose of low production costs in the patent specification.

In summary, the high-temperature water crystallization in step (3) of claim 1 of this patent, based on its specific limitations and the content of the specification, should normally be understood as using water as a solvent to achieve purification through the crystallization of the dicarboxylic acid. However, given the low solubility of long-chain dicarboxylic acids in water, the crystallization process described in step (3) is technically illogical and has no practical significance in production. Therefore, a person skilled in the art cannot reasonably determine the specific meaning of the high-temperature water crystallization in step (3) of claim 1 of this patent. Moreover, if the high-temperature water crystallization in step (3) were understood as a non-conventional crystallization process, it would contradict the characteristics of the high-temperature water crystallization in step (2). Consequently, this claim does not meet the requirement of Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law that claims shall clearly define the scope of patent protection sought. Based on substantially the same reasons, the specification of this patent also does not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

During the first instance, the CNIPA and Cathay Biotech argued that because the material used in step (3) is an impure dicarboxylic acid, including residual solvents, water, and unremoved impurities from the previous step, the "high-temperature water crystallization" in this step should not be a conventional recrystallization process in which "water is used as a solvent, and the dicarboxylic acid is completely dissolved in water and then precipitated again through cooling crystallization." In response, the court of first instance held that: First, as stated above, based on the limitations of steps (3) and (2) of claim 1 and the content of the patent specification, step (3) should be a conventional crystallization operation using water as a solvent to achieve purification through crystallization of the dicarboxylic acid. Second, the appealed decision recorded that "the patentee also argued during the oral proceedings that in this step, the dicarboxylic acid is actually in a dispersed state of 'partial dissolution-melting-suspension.'" However, Decision No. 42594 recorded that "the patentee confirmed that there is no melting situation in step (3) of claim 1 of this patent." Furthermore, during the oral proceedings of the invalidation request corresponding to Decision No. 42594, when responding to the question "How is step (3) supposed to remove solvent impurities?" Cathay Biotech stated: "The function of step (3) is to remove the solvent. The high temperature is to increase the solubility of the dicarboxylic acid and further remove impurities mixed with acetic acid from step (2). The feed ratio refers to the subsequent centrifugation process, generally allowing centrifugation to proceed smoothly. High-temperature water crystallization is not to completely dissolve the dicarboxylic acid and then crystallize it out." It can be seen that in the above invalidation request, Cathay Biotech described step (3) as "further removing impurities mixed with acetic acid from step (2)" and "high-temperature water crystallization is not to completely dissolve the dicarboxylic acid and then crystallize it out," which are different purification process operations from the high-temperature water crystallization described in step (2) of claim 1. Cathay Biotech has expressed different and even contradictory understandings of the process of step (3) in different proceedings. In summary, the above arguments of the CNIPA and Cathay Biotech cannot clarify the meaning of the high-temperature water crystallization in step (3) of claim 1. Their arguments lack factual and legal basis and are not supported.

Furthermore, the court of first instance held that, given the above determination that claim 1 of this patent does not comply with Article 26, Paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, the appealed decision's finding that claim 1 complies with Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law is clearly inappropriate and should also be corrected in accordance with the law.

In summary, the court of first instance entered the following judgment: 1. The appealed decision is revoked; 2. The CNIPA shall make a new examination decision on the invalidation request filed by Hanlin Company against this patent. The court acceptance fee for the first instance of RMB 100 shall be borne by the CNIPA.

This Court's opinions on the evidence: The content of Evidence 1 and Evidence 2 submitted by Hanlin Company consists of common general knowledge that has already been asserted in the invalidation declaration examination procedure and was not disputed by any party. Evidence 3 is evidence submitted by Cathay Biotech in another separate infringement lawsuit, and its main content still relates to facts not disputed by Cathay Biotech. Whether Hanlin Company submits these three pieces of evidence in the second instance does not affect this Court's judgment on whether Hanlin Company's related claims can be established. Furthermore, considering that Evidence 1 is not prior art relative to this patent, the publication date of Evidence 2 cannot be confirmed, and Evidence 3 is not relevant to its purpose of proof, this Court will not admit the above Evidence 1 to 3 submitted by Hanlin Company. The facts recorded in Evidence 4 have already been found in the first instance judgment, and the first instance judgment has used them as a basis for its decision, so they are not new evidence.

(I) Dispute over the inventor designation of this patent

According to the second instance evidence 3 to 5 submitted by the CNIPA, on April 30, 2010, Hanlin Company applied for this patent to the CNIPA. The inventors listed on the application documents were: Huang Li, Liu Shuangjiang, Cao Wubo, Wang Zhizhou, Ge Minghua, Chen Yuantong, and Fu Shenzhan. On January 5, 2012, Lei Guang and Li Naiqiang filed a lawsuit with the Beijing First Intermediate People's Court, alleging: Lei Guang and Li Naiqiang were scientific research and technical personnel of Shandong Cathay Biotech Materials Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shandong Cathay) and Cathay Biotech, respectively, and both participated in the development of standardized operating procedures and subsequent optimization experiments for the biological production technology of long-chain dicarboxylic acids. Wang Zhizhou and Ge Minghua had worked at Shandong Cathay and had access to relevant technical drawings, equipment, and production processes. In July 2008, Wang Zhizhou resigned from Shandong Cathay and had become a shareholder of Hanlin Company before that. On December 23, 2008, Hanlin Company added "Research and development, production, sales, and import/export business of long-chain dicarboxylic acids and series products" to its business scope and applied for this patent on April 30, 2010. This patent is identical to the standardized operating procedures for the biological production technology of long-chain dicarboxylic acids used by Shandong Cathay, and its core process parameters are the same as those in Cathay Biotech's already granted Patent No. 200610029784.6. Lei Guang and Li Naiqiang made substantive contributions to the above technical solution and are the inventors of this patent application, entitled to the right of attribution. The seven defendants including Wang Zhizhou did not make substantive contributions, and their acts of impersonation and plagiarism infringed upon the right of attribution of Lei Guang and Li Naiqiang. Therefore, they requested the court to confirm that the inventors of this patent application are Lei Guang and Li Naiqiang.

In that case, Lei Guang and Li Naiqiang submitted a key piece of evidence to prove they were the actual inventors, namely the 2003 SOP, which recorded a method for refining long-chain dicarboxylic acids that is substantially the same as the technical solution defined in claim 1 of this patent.
